A1-A2.headline: The Amazing Medieval Map Called the Catalan Atlas

pages.text: Have you ever wondered how sailors found their way across the ocean long ago? The Catalan Atlas, made in the 1300s, was a guide for travelers. This beautiful map helped people understand the world.
pages.caption: Original leaves of the Catalan Atlas.

evidence.articleCaption: Montage of 8 pages (the third to sixth leaves) of the original 1375 Catalan Atlas

pages.text: The first parts of the map contain important texts about astronomy and the shape of the Earth. Sailors used these texts to help them find their way at night. The map explains how to tell time using the stars. It also gives tips on how to watch the tides. These details were very helpful for people who traveled on ships across the sea. The map shows that people in the past were very smart and observed the world around them with great care.
The map shows many cities with different flags to show who rules them. Jerusalem is placed near the center of the map. It was created by Cresques Abraham, a skilled Jewish mapmaker from Majorca.
pages.caption: Ruler depicted in the atlas.

pages.text: The atlas includes detailed drawings of places in Asia and Africa. It shows important rulers and ships. These drawings helped people in Europe learn about the wider world during medieval times. The map shows many cities with different flags to show who rules them. These pictures were very important for people who wanted to know about lands far away. It was a window into a world that many people had never seen before in their lives.

B1-B2.headline: Exploring the History and Geography of the Catalan Atlas

pages.text: Imagine holding a map that guided explorers across the medieval world. The Catalan Atlas, created around 1375, is a masterpiece of history. It reveals how people once viewed the vast, mysterious globe.
pages.caption: Original leaves of the Catalan Atlas.

evidence.articleCaption: Montage of 8 pages (the third to sixth leaves) of the original 1375 Catalan Atlas

pages.text: The initial leaves contain detailed texts regarding cosmography, astronomy, and astrology. These sections highlight the spherical nature of the Earth and offer practical guidance for sailors navigating by night and measuring tides. Scholars note that the depiction of Mansa Musa as the richest man in the region is considered by some historians to be an early European stage in the fabrication of the Mansa Musa wealth myth (P8).

Comprising six vellum leaves painted with gold and silver, the atlas places Jerusalem near its geographical center. The map utilizes symbols and flags to denote political allegiances across various Christian and non-Christian cities.
pages.caption: Depiction of a sovereign ruler.

imageProvenance.credit: attributed to Abraham Cresques attributed to Abraham Cresques
imageProvenance.imageAttribution: attributed to Abraham Cresques attributed to Abraham Cresques (Public domain)

evidence.fileTitle: File:Catalan Atlas BNF Sheet 6 Mansa Musa.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Depiction of Mansa Musa, ruler of the Mali Empire, holding a gold object

pages.text: Furthermore, the eastern sections incorporate travel literature from figures like Marco Polo, detailing local economies and customs. The western portion features early compass roses, aiding maritime navigation across the known world. The map also depicts the western part of the Indian subcontinent, accurately showing the Delhi Sultanate and the Yadava capital of Deogiri, which provides a window into medieval trade networks (P14, P16).

C1-C2.headline: Scholarly Interpretations and Historical Context of the Catalan Atlas

pages.text: The Catalan Atlas, dated to 1375, represents the zenith of medieval cartography. This foundational artifact synthesizes geographical knowledge with artistic execution.
pages.caption: Original leaves of the Catalan Atlas.

evidence.articleCaption: Montage of 8 pages (the third to sixth leaves) of the original 1375 Catalan Atlas

pages.text: Beyond its cartographic representation, the atlas engages in complex socio-political framing. Scholarly analysis reveals that certain portrayals, such as Mansa Musa's wealth, contributed significantly to early European myth-making processes.
pages.caption: Depiction of Mansa Musa.

imageProvenance.credit: attributed to Abraham Cresques attributed to Abraham Cresques
imageProvenance.imageAttribution: attributed to Abraham Cresques attributed to Abraham Cresques (Public domain)

evidence.fileTitle: File:Catalan Atlas BNF Sheet 6 Mansa Musa.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Depiction of Mansa Musa, ruler of the Mali Empire, holding a gold object

pages.text: Interpretations of regional entities like Organa remain multifaceted. Researchers debate whether Organa represents the Kanem-Bornu Empire, Ouargla, or an alternative attribution like the Ife Empire, highlighting medieval cartographic limitations. Furthermore, the map provides a clear depiction of the western Indian subcontinent, identifying the Delhi Sultanate and the capital of Deogiri, which serves as a critical reference for understanding medieval geopolitical boundaries (P14, P16).

Integrating travel accounts from Marco Polo and missionary reports, the atlas meticulously delineates eastern trade networks, maritime technology, and geopolitical domains. This reflects an intricate worldview of fourteenth-century Europe, where the map served as both a practical navigational tool and a symbolic representation of power, wealth, and the distant, often misunderstood, regions of the known world during that era.
